metadata.note: CORRECTED after the map showed this line skipping Dayton, which prompted a closer check: the original version of this file traced the route through Xenia and Loveland, following the Little Miami Railroad's bed (now the Little Miami Scenic Trail). That was a real historical railroad, but it belonged to the wrong company -- the Little Miami Railroad and Columbus & Xenia Railroad were leased in 1870 to the Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and St. Louis Railway, part of the PENNSYLVANIA RAILROAD system, not the Big Four / New York Central. The actual Cleveland-Cincinnati route belonging to the Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati and Indianapolis Railway ('the Bee Line', formed 1868) and its 1889 successor the Big Four ran via Dayton: in 1871 the CCC&I leased the Cincinnati & Springfield Railroad (Cincinnati through the Mill Creek Valley via Ivorydale Junction and Middletown to Dayton) and the Cincinnati, Sandusky & Cleveland Railroad (Dayton to Springfield), finally completing a through route from Cincinnati to Columbus and Cleveland under its own control. Geometry now traces this real Dayton route (Cleveland-Shelby-Galion-Delaware-Columbus-Springfield-Dayton-Middletown-Ivorydale-Cincinnati), sourced from real OpenStreetMap active-rail geometry the entire way -- unlike the Xenia route, this Dayton corridor never lost its active freight service, so there were no trail-tracing gaps to work around. The 'Bee Line' feature's start date has been moved from 1851 to 1871 to match when this company actually owned a through line to Cincinnati; before that, CC&C's Cincinnati traffic moved via an interchange partnership over the (competing, Pennsylvania-affiliated) Little Miami/Columbus & Xenia route, which is not this company's own trackage and so isn't depicted as this feature's geometry. The western 'Bee Line' reach (Cleveland-Indianapolis-Chicago) is unaffected by this correction and remains real-traced as before. Frequencies are estimated/unsourced except where noted. Notably, unlike the NYC Water Level Route (see new_york_central.geojson), this corridor was NOT continued by Amtrak in 1971 -- there is no direct Cleveland-Cincinnati passenger train today, visible by comparing against amtrak.geojson on this same map. ADDED 2026-08-18: a fourth feature completing the Big Four's namesake fourth city, Indianapolis-Terre Haute-St. Louis (the Indianapolis and St. Louis Railway, 1870), real-traced via OpenStreetMap/Overpass; carried the Southwestern Limited 1889-1966, then Amtrak's National Limited 1971-1979 (see amtrak_national_limited.geojson, not duplicated here).

metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.nyc_company_split: 2026-08-24: compound "predecessor / New York Central Railroad" company strings split per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. The legend groups on the exact company string (app.js railroadsInView), so a compound string drew as a separate railroad from the New York Central even for years the NYC itself ran the trains. Each feature is now split at the date its own segment note names the new operator, into features with identical geometry: the predecessor keeps its name and colour for the earlier years, and the NYC-operated years become "New York Central Railroad" at #5C677D. The Pittsburgh and Lake Erie and the Big Four were renamed but NOT split -- both were NYC-controlled yet stayed separately operated railroads under their own names, so they keep their own legend row.
